newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Chubais says Russian budget not realistic.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Chubais says Russian budget not realistic.

text.p: Russia's reform chief, dismissing the 1997 budget as unrealistic, promised on Thursday to cut spending across the board and raise over $5 billion through state sell-offs and precious metals sales.

Anatoly Chubais, finance minister and one of two first deputy prime ministers in the new government, told the upper house of parliament that taxes brought in a mere 39 percent of planned income in the first quarter, although higher than expected customs revenues had made up some of the gap.

"The monstrous budget crisis is at the root of all the troubles and it throws into question whether the state can perform its functions," he said. "It is not possible to finance all scheduled payments under these circumstances."
He added: "We have to recognise that it is not possible to fulfil this budget."
Russian debt prices eased on the comments.

"Chubais's comments about the budget were a bit unnerving. But the market generally is subdued and rather pessimistic as it waits for further data," said John Bunner, deputy director of asset trading at Moscow Narodny in London.

Russian ministers have long highlighted low tax revenues and huge wage and pension arrears as Russia's most pressing economic problems, and they say the budget, forced through parliament earlier this year, needs to be revised.
But officials in the State Duma lower house of parliament said discussion of new spending levels would take only place on May 21 -- a full month after the expiry of an official deadline.

Chubais had originally been due to outline the plans and review the first quarter budget on April 23, but the officials said the debate had been delayed at the request of Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
The budget law says the debate should take place within 20 days of the end of the quarter.
The lower house is dominated by conservatives and many deputies have said they are unlikely to approve spending cuts.

The International Monetary Fund has delayed several tranches of a $10 billion three-year loan to Russia because it is worried about low revenues, although IMF head Michel Camdessus has said he is ready to recommend Russia's 1997-98 economic programme.
A string of government decrees and the creation of an emergency commission to force tax debtors to pay have done little to bring in extra funds.
The new head of the State Tax Service, Alexander Pochinok, promised in an interview with Kommersant Daily newspaper on Thursday that he would be tougher than his predecessors.
"In my opinion the State Tax Service has adopted too mild a policy," said Pochinok, previously a senior official in the State Duma lower house of parliament.

"We need to be much tougher... The moment a taxpayer has money and refuses to pay, we need to exact this money in a tough way. The tax service has to be strong enough to obtain what it is entitled to by law."
Chubais said the government would raise an extra 30 trillion roubles ($5.2 billion) through privatisation and on shares and precious metals markets.

It was not clear exactly how Chubais, who has already targeted higher privatisation revenues this year, expects to raise this money. But sales of gold and diamonds are traditionally a way to bring money to state coffers.
He said the government would finish work on a new tax code on Thursday and the document would be submitted to the Duma.
"We will do everything we can to get it accepted, but we cannot guarantee that it will be passed in time for the 1998 budget to be drawn up on the basis of this code," he said.
Camdessus has said the IMF will not hand over any extra funds until the government approves the tax code, aimed at making Russia's convoluted tax system simpler and more workable.
($ = 5749 Russian roubles)
